p.src: The Minimum Is Technical

u.src: The Minimum Is Technical
en: The Minimum Is Technical

p.src: The theoretical minimum is not a list of conclusions stated in words. It is the least mathematics needed to move reliably to the next subject, which in this case is general relativity and then cosmology. No advanced machinery is required tonight, but the calculations must be followed patiently. Index placement, transformation laws, and contractions are not decoration; they are the grammar in which curved geometry is written.

p.src:
Let $x^{m}$ and $y^{m}$ be two coordinate systems on the same space. A covariant vector transforms as $V_{m}^{(y)}(y)
  =
  \frac{\partial x^{n}}{\partial y^{m}}
  V_{n}^{(x)}(x),$ whereas a contravariant vector transforms as $W_{(y)}^{m}(y)
  =
  \frac{\partial y^{m}}{\partial x^{n}}
  W_{(x)}^{n}(x).$ The free index $m$ appears on both sides and belongs to the $y$ description. The repeated $n$ is summed and belongs to the $x$ description.

p.src: A collection of numbers is not a vector merely because it can be arranged as an arrow. Temperature, pressure, and humidity are three scalars. Putting their numerical values along three axes does not make a geometric vector, because those values do not mix under a coordinate change according to Eq.  or Eq. . Transformation behavior defines the object.

p.src: Coordinates conventionally carry upper indices. A coordinate in the denominator of a derivative therefore contributes a lower index, while a coordinate differential naturally carries an upper one. The convention is arbitrary, but once adopted it makes the Jacobian patterns difficult to misread.

p.src: Raising and Lowering Indices

u.src: Raising and Lowering Indices
en: Raising and Lowering Indices

p.src:
The metric now links the two vector descriptions: $V_{n}=g_{nm}V^{m},
  \qquad
  V^{m}=g^{mn}V_{n}.$ The first equation lowers an index and the second raises it. Because the metric is invertible, either set of components determines the other. In geometric terms, $V_{n}$ is the covector obtained by taking the metric inner product of $V$ with each coordinate basis vector. In an orthonormal basis this reduces to the familiar projection picture.

p.src: Tensors can be added only when their index types agree. The sum $T_{mn}+W_{mn}$ transforms coherently; a formal sum of $T_{mn}$ and $W^{mn}$ does not.

u.src: Tensors can be added only when their index types agree. The sum $T_{mn}+W_{mn}$ transforms coherently; a formal sum of $T_{mn}$ and $W^{mn}$ does not.
en: Tensors can be added only when their index types agree. The sum $T_{mn}+W_{mn}$ transforms coherently; a formal sum of $T_{mn}$ and $W^{mn}$ does not.

p.src: If every component of a tensor vanishes in one coordinate system, every component vanishes in all coordinate systems, because each transformed component is a linear combination of zeros. Hence if $T_{mn}=W_{mn}$ in one chart, then $T_{mn}-W_{mn}=0$ there and therefore everywhere. Tensor equality is geometric even though the separate components depend on coordinates.

p.src: A First Expanding-Spacetime Metric

u.src: A First Expanding-Spacetime Metric
en: A First Expanding-Spacetime Metric

p.src:
For a homogeneous and isotropic flat spatial geometry, choose comoving coordinates and write $(g_{\mu\nu})
  =
  \begin{pmatrix}
    1&0&0&0\\
    0&-a^{2}(t)&0&0\\
    0&0&-a^{2}(t)&0\\
    0&0&0&-a^{2}(t)
  \end{pmatrix}.$ The corresponding interval is $\boxed{
  d\tau^{2}
  =
  dt^{2}
  -
  a^{2}(t)\left(dx^{2}+dy^{2}+dz^{2}\right).}$ The single function $a(t)$ is the scale factor. At a fixed cosmic time, two comoving points separated by coordinate distance $\Delta\ell_{\rm com}$ have physical distance $\Delta\ell_{\rm phys}(t)
  =
  a(t)\,\Delta\ell_{\rm com}.$ If $a(t)$ grows, the physical separation grows even while the comoving coordinates remain fixed.

p.src:
For the flat plane, $f(r)=r$. For a unit sphere, $f(r)=\sin r,
  \qquad
  ds^{2}=dr^{2}+\sin^{2}r\,d\theta^{2}.$ The circles grow from one pole to the equator and then shrink toward the other pole.

p.src: These surfaces vary with position $r$; the cosmological metric varies with time $t$. The analogy is not yet a curvature calculation. Its purpose is to make metric coefficients readable as geometry. The next steps are parallel transport, curvature, and eventually Einstein’s field equations.
